newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Jamaica, U.S. disagree over boarding fishing ship.
newsitem.headline: Jamaica, U.S. disagree over boarding fishing ship.

text.p: A war of words has broken out between the United States and Jamaica over the alleged boarding of a Jamaican fishing vessel by U.S. and British sailors as part of the U.S. drug war in the Caribbean.

A strongly worded U.S. Embassy statement on Tuesday night accused the Kingston government of behaving in a provocative way over the incident and virtually accused it of lying. The dispute was the latest between the two countries over how the United States wages the drug war in Caribbean waters.

Jamaica said the fishing boat Silver Dollar was stopped by the British Royal Navy ship Liverpool last month and boarded by British and U.S. personnel who reportedly searched the vessel but found nothing incriminating.

It said on June 27 that it had called in the U.S. and British ambassadors to demand an apology. It said the search took place in Jamaican territorial waters without government permission and it would seek compensation for the fishermen.

The U.S. Embassy denied a search had taken place. "At no point was the Silver Dollar detained or directed to stop ... at no point did British or U.S. personnel attempt to board or search the fishing vessel," it said.

U.S. Ambassador J. Gary Cooper did not meet Jamaica's Foreign Minister Seymour Mullings until Tuesday, the embassy said. It said the Foreign Ministry's attitude to the incident was "provocative" and accused Kingston of listening only to the fishermen's side of the story.

"We have exercised considerable restraint in regard to public actions by the Jamaican government. This includes the issuance of a provocative press release containing factual errors ... and repeated references to a meeting with ambassador Cooper that never took place," the embassy said.

The dispute appeared to bring U.S.-Jamaican relations to a new low following a disagreement last year over Kingston's refusal to sign an accord that would allow U.S. drug enforcement agents to detain and search vessels in Jamaica's waters and airspace -- the so-called Ship Rider accords.

A senior U.S. State Department official threatened Jamaica with decertification as a drug war ally and claimed to have knowledge of a Jamaican political figure with strong links to drug traffickers. The statement was later retracted.
Kingston and Washington agreed on a final text this year but the accord has yet to come into force.
Washington is concerned that Colombian cocaine and heroin traffickers have opened up new smuggling routes to the United States through the islands and sea lanes of the Caribbean.
